prompt:
Our nightly report scheduler misbehaves around clock changes. Customers in Europe/Berlin with a daily 09:00 report got it at 10:00 on March 29 this year, and at 08:00 last October 26 — and each time it quietly went back to normal on its own the following day. The relevant function (Python 3.11, zoneinfo, timestamps stored as naive UTC in Postgres):

```python
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone
from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo

def next_run(last_run: datetime, hour: int, tz: ZoneInfo) -> datetime:
    # last_run is naive UTC from the DB
    offset = last_run.replace(tzinfo=timezone.utc).astimezone(tz).utcoffset()
    local = last_run + offset  # local wall time, kept naive
    nxt = local.replace(hour=hour, minute=0, second=0, microsecond=0)
    if nxt <= local:
        nxt = nxt + timedelta(days=1)
    return nxt - offset  # back to naive UTC
```

The returned value is written back to the DB and a worker fires when `now() >= next_run`. This function is called from three other modules, so the signature must stay exactly as is, and we can't add dependencies (no pytz, no pendulum). Find the root cause, fix it, and give me a couple of concrete datetimes I can use in a regression test to prove the fix.

The fix performs the conversion with the timezone attached to the target datetime — e.g. build the aware local time via astimezone(tz), set the hour, add a day if needed, and convert back with astimezone(timezone.utc) — while keeping the exact signature and naive-UTC return, and supplies test datetimes straddling 2026-03-29 for Europe/Berlin (e.g. last_run 2026-03-28 08:00 UTC must yield 2026-03-29 07:00 UTC, i.e. 09:00 CEST).

Rewrites the scheduler around a cron library or croniter, violating the no-new-dependencies constraint

Card number
Invalid
Expiry
CVC
Pay now

- Ops dashboard project: design review last quarter rejected gauge widgets as 'casino-looking'; stakeholders agreed number tiles + trend sparklines for KPIs.

prompt: Our marketing site's CSS has rotted over three years of contractors. Consolidates to at most 8 gray tokens and at most 6 font-size steps, with explicit values given

prompt: We're an EU-based e-commerce shop and our order-confirmation email is a mess — it currently renders as one giant PNG of the receipt, which Gmail clips and Outlook shows as a broken-image icon because images are blocked by default. Puts prices or the cancellation notice inside images, recreating the images-blocked failure
Forgets one legal element — VAT as a separate line, or reduces the withdrawal notice to a link
Ignores dark mode or 'solves' it with a technique Gmail strips (media-query-only with no fallback thinking)
Adds JavaScript, embedded video, or interactive AMP-for-email components that these clients block

All order details and legal content are specified as live HTML text, with images limited to non-essential branding carrying alt text
The answer explicitly states the email remains fully readable/usable with images blocked
Price breakdown includes unit prices, shipping, and VAT as separate line items, and the 14-day withdrawal notice appears as body text

Dark mode is addressed with at least one concretely named technique (e.g. prefers-color-scheme media query, meta color-scheme declaration, or dark-safe color choices that survive client color inversion)
No JavaScript, external CSS files, or web-font dependence for critical text is proposed

memory_snapshot:
- Transactional email stack: sent via our own SMTP through the order service; templates are static HTML strings, no templating engine changes allowed this quarter.
- Past lesson: a promo email using background-image hero shipped invisible CTA text in Outlook 2019 — support tickets spiked; team rule since then is 'critical content is never on an image'.
- Brand team accepts system font stack in email; the custom brand font is web-only.
- Legal flagged us once before for VAT shown as 'incl.' instead of a separate line — Finance now audits every customer-facing receipt format.
- Analytics: ~41% of our customers open email in Gmail mobile, ~22% Outlook desktop (B2B buyers), ~19% Apple Mail.

prompt: We run a 4-person B2B SaaS support team. Our support agent (an LLM with tool access, but for this design treat it as a text spec) handles ~60 tickets/day and keeps forgetting things it already learned: known bugs, per-customer quirks, workarounds that were superseded. We want persistent memory, but our platform team vetoed any new infrastructure: memory must live as plain markdown files in the existing git repo, retrieved by filename and text search only — no database, no embeddings service, no background workers. Design the memory system: the file/folder layout, what qualifies as worth writing (and what must never be written), how the agent finds the right note at ticket time, and how stale or superseded entries are handled so old workarounds stop resurfacing. Keep the whole spec practical enough that we could implement it this sprint.
expected_behavior: A compact file-based memory schema: a small folder layout with an index file, explicit write-worthiness criteria (durable facts, decisions, per-customer quirks; never secrets/PII/one-off details), a cheap retrieval path (index + grep by customer/component), and a concrete staleness mechanism (supersede-in-place or status/date fields) rather than unbounded append.
failure_modes: Smuggles in vetoed infrastructure (SQLite, vector DB, embeddings, a cron service) despite the plain-markdown constraint
Defines what to store but no retrieval discipline, leaving 'grep everything' as the implicit plan
Append-only design with no supersede/expiry story, so the stated stale-workaround problem is unsolved
No exclusion rules — customer PII and credentials end up eligible for memory files
Over-elaborate taxonomy (10+ folders, YAML ontologies) that a 4-person team would never maintain
automatic_checks: Storage is markdown/plain files only; introduces no database, vector store, embedding service, or background worker
States explicit criteria for what gets written to memory AND at least one category that must never be written (e.g. secrets or customer PII)
Describes a concrete retrieval mechanism using filenames/index/text-search, not semantic search
Includes a specific mechanism for marking or removing stale/superseded entries
Includes an index or entry-point file so lookup does not require scanning every note
human_review_notes: Check whether the staleness/supersession mechanism would actually stop an old workaround from being retrieved, not just label it.
memory_snapshot:
- Support repo already has `docs/runbooks/` in git; team resisted a wiki migration last quarter — anything new must live beside runbooks.
- Past incident: an agent pasted a customer's API key into a shared doc; compliance now requires an explicit deny-list for stored content.
- Team convention: every durable doc starts with a 3-line frontmatter (owner, updated, status) — docs without it get ignored.
- Earlier experiment with per-ticket auto-notes produced 900 files in a month; nobody could find anything and the folder was abandoned. Lesson: most tickets are not worth remembering.
- Grep-based lookup was fast enough on the runbooks folder (<200 files); no one wants embeddings for this.

prompt: Our internal policy-QA assistant answers HR and compliance questions over 340 PDF policy documents. Pipeline today: PDFs converted to text, split into fixed 512-token chunks with 64-token overlap, embedded once, stored in pgvector, retrieval = top-3 by cosine similarity, answer generated from those 3 chunks. Users report two recurring failures: (1) questions about exceptions are answered with the general rule — the exceptions live in footnotes and tables that the converter flattens into surrounding prose; (2) questions naming a specific policy number ('per HR-114, can a contractor...') often retrieve chunks from the wrong policy entirely. Constraints: we can afford exactly one full re-processing/re-embedding pass, we cannot add new infrastructure beyond what Postgres/pgvector already gives us, and no model fine-tuning. Diagnose why each failure happens and specify the revised pipeline, including how you'd verify the fixes actually worked before rollout.
expected_behavior: A diagnosis tying failure 1 to structure-blind conversion/chunking (footnotes and tables severed from the rules they modify) and failure 2 to embeddings' weakness on exact identifiers; fixes within constraints — structure-aware chunking with policy-ID metadata attached to every chunk, metadata/keyword filtering (Postgres full-text or ILIKE on policy number) combined with vector search, done in the single allowed re-processing pass — plus a small labeled eval set of known-failure questions run before/after.
failure_modes: Reaches for banned solutions: a reranker service, Elasticsearch, LlamaIndex, fine-tuning, or a second embedding model
Only tunes retrieval parameters (top-k, overlap) without addressing that the chunks themselves sever exceptions from rules
Ignores the policy-number failure or hand-waves it as 'better embeddings' instead of exact-match metadata filtering
Proposes iterative re-embedding experiments, violating the single re-processing pass budget
No concrete verification plan — declares the fix correct without an eval set built from the reported failures
automatic_checks: Attributes failure 1 to chunking/conversion destroying document structure (footnotes/tables separated from their rules), not to the embedding model or LLM
Attributes failure 2 to semantic similarity being unreliable for exact identifiers and proposes exact/keyword or metadata filtering on policy number using Postgres capabilities
Introduces no new infrastructure, service, or fine-tuning; all changes fit Postgres/pgvector plus the ingestion code
Revised pipeline fits within one re-processing/re-embedding pass, stated explicitly
Includes a verification step using a test set derived from the reported failure cases, evaluated before rollout
human_review_notes: Scrutinize whether the hybrid retrieval design (vector + policy-number filter) is concretely specified for pgvector/Postgres rather than gestured at with tool names.
memory_snapshot:
- This pgvector instance is shared with two other apps; DBA approval needed for extensions beyond what's installed (vector, pg_trgm already enabled).
- Previous chunking rework on the sales-docs bot: naive re-chunk without an eval set shipped a regression that took 3 weeks to notice. Rule since: build the failure-question list FIRST.
- Policy docs follow a house format: policy ID in the header of every page, exceptions always in a 'Notwithstanding' clause or a footnote.
- The PDF converter (pdfminer-based) is ours to modify; it already emits page-level metadata we currently throw away.
- Compliance requires answers to cite the policy ID they came from.

prompt: I lead platform at a 40-engineer fintech. We have ~1,200 internal docs (Confluence exports, ADRs, runbooks, onboarding guides) and engineers keep asking the same questions in Slack. Refuses to commit — presents all three options 'depending on your needs' with no recommendation
Scopes v1 beyond two engineer-weeks (custom chunking pipeline + reranker + chat UI + evaluation harness all at once)
Success criteria are vague ('user satisfaction') with no measurable golden-set or metric
Ignores the 1,200-doc scale, arguing for vector infrastructure as if the corpus were millions of documents
automatic_checks: Commits to exactly one recommended v1 approach and names it explicitly
Compares at least keyword/BM25 and vector approaches with concrete trade-offs for this corpus size
All proposed tooling is self-hostable; no hosted/SaaS API (OpenAI, Cohere, Pinecone, etc.) appears in the recommended plan
Defines at least one quantifiable success metric measurable within the two-week review (e.g. golden-question hit rate)
States explicit conditions that would trigger the next investment stage
human_review_notes: Judge whether the recommendation is genuinely sized to one engineer for two weeks, or a disguised multi-quarter RAG platform.
memory_snapshot:
- Company infra standard: everything deploys as containers on the internal Nomad cluster; new stateful services need an ops review (~1 week lead time).
- Last year's 'AI wiki bot' pilot died because nobody defined success; leadership now asks 'what's the metric?' in every review.
- The Slack #ask-platform channel history is exportable — a prior analysis found ~30 questions cover 70% of asks.

prompt: Continuing work on our audit-log service (Node 20, Postgres 15, no ORM — hand-written SQL). Decisions already settled in earlier sessions, not up for debate: (a) audit rows are immutable and soft-delete only via a `redacted_at` column; (b) all list endpoints use keyset (cursor) pagination on `(created_at, id)` — offset pagination was tried and reverted for drift under load; (c) the events table is partitioned monthly by `created_at`; (d) retention: 24 months hot, then archive. Today's task: design the monthly archival job that moves partitions older than 24 months to cold storage (S3 parquet) and drops them from Postgres. Cover: job scheduling and idempotency (it may be re-run after partial failure), how reads for archived ranges behave at the API (we don't need to serve them live, but the API must not lie), and the verification step before a partition is dropped. Flag anything genuinely still open, but don't reopen the settled decisions.
expected_behavior: An archival job design that visibly builds on the settled decisions — operates on whole monthly partitions, exports to parquet, verifies (row-count/checksum) before DETACH/DROP, is idempotent via a state/manifest record, and defines API behavior for out-of-range cursors (explicit 'archived' response, not silent empty pages). Open questions are flagged narrowly (e.g. redacted rows in archives) without re-litigating pagination or immutability.
failure_modes: Re-litigates settled decisions — proposes offset pagination for the archive reader or hard deletes, contradicting the stated context
Drops partitions before any verification that the S3 export is complete and readable
No idempotency story: re-running after partial failure double-exports or drops an unarchived partition
API behavior hand-waved — archived time ranges silently return empty results, which 'lies' exactly as the prompt forbids
Introduces heavyweight new infrastructure (Airflow, Kafka, a lakehouse) for a monthly single-tenant job
automatic_checks: Archival unit is the monthly partition (uses the existing partitioning), not row-by-row copying
Includes an explicit verification step (row count and/or checksum comparison) before the Postgres partition is dropped
Describes idempotent re-run behavior after partial failure, with some persisted job state or manifest
Specifies API behavior for requests into archived ranges that is explicit (status/flag/message), not silently empty
Does not contradict any settled decision: no offset pagination, no hard deletes of audit rows, no mutation of existing rows other than the existing redaction mechanism
human_review_notes: Verify the answer treats the four settled decisions as load-bearing inputs to the design rather than boilerplate it restates and then ignores.
memory_snapshot:
- Audit-log service conventions: plain `pg` client, migrations via node-pg-migrate, jobs run from a single `jobs/` folder triggered by systemd timers — team rejected Airflow twice.
- The offset-pagination revert (PR #212) burned a week; anyone proposing OFFSET on this service gets pushback.
- S3 bucket `audit-cold` already exists with object-lock (compliance WORM); writes there are effectively immutable.
- Prior lesson from the billing archiver: always DETACH the partition and keep it 7 days before DROP — saved us once.
- Legal has an open thread on whether `redacted_at` rows may be exported to cold storage at all; unresolved as of last session.

prompt: We operate a long-running AI assistant for a European telco's customer-care line. It keeps per-customer memory across calls so agents don't re-ask everything: preferences, past issues, promised follow-ups. Memory grows without bound and we inject it into the model at call start — budget: at most 4,000 tokens of memory per call, total. Design the memory lifecycle policy: what gets written after each call, how and when raw entries are compacted into summaries, how the 4,000-token injection is selected when a customer has years of history, and retention. Two hard requirements from legal: (1) GDPR right-to-erasure — when a customer requests deletion of a specific incident, it must disappear from raw entries AND from any summary derived from it, so the design must make that traceable; (2) payment card numbers and government IDs must never enter memory in any form. Describe the policy precisely enough that an engineer could implement the write, compact, select, and erase paths.
expected_behavior: A four-path lifecycle: gated writes with a redaction/deny-list step before persistence; tiered compaction (raw entries → periodic summaries) where every summary records provenance links to its source entries so erasure can cascade via re-summarization from surviving sources; a selection strategy for the 4k budget (recency + open follow-ups + relevance, with a stable priority order and truncation rule); and explicit retention windows. Erasure is designed as delete-sources-then-rebuild-derived, not best-effort editing of summaries.
failure_modes: Summaries have no provenance links to source entries, making right-to-erasure from derived summaries impossible — the central trap of the task
Handles erasure by 'asking the model to remove the fact from the summary' instead of deterministic delete-and-rebuild
PII requirement met with vague 'we filter sensitive data' instead of a concrete pre-write redaction step for card numbers/IDs
Selection policy ignores the 4,000-token cap or has no defined priority/truncation order when history exceeds it
Over-architecture: multi-region event-sourced memory platform with vector DB, stream processors, and ML classifiers for a policy-design question
automatic_checks: Every summary/compacted artifact carries traceable references to the raw entries it was derived from
Erasure path deletes the raw entries and regenerates (not hand-edits) any summaries derived from them
Specifies a redaction/validation step BEFORE anything is persisted, explicitly covering card numbers and government IDs
Defines a deterministic selection/priority scheme for filling the 4,000-token injection budget, including what is dropped first when over budget
States concrete retention periods or expiry rules for at least raw entries and summaries
human_review_notes: Focus on the erasure-through-summaries mechanism: does the provenance model actually make cascade deletion implementable, or is it asserted without a workable data structure?
memory_snapshot:
- Telco client's DPO signs off on all memory features; last review rejected a design because deletion from derived data was 'not demonstrable' — auditability beat cleverness.
- Existing stack: memory rows in Postgres with a `source_call_id` column already on every entry; team prefers extending this over new stores.
- Prior incident: an IBAN appeared in a call summary; fix was a regex+Luhn pre-write scrubber, now considered the pattern for structured PII.
- Ops constraint: compaction jobs run nightly in a fixed maintenance window; nothing may run per-call except the write path.
- Product finding: agents mostly need open follow-ups and the last 3 interactions; deep history is rarely read.

prompt: We're a B2B SaaS (HR payroll, ~900 tickets/week) and want to automate first-line support triage with an LLM agent. Requirements: classify each ticket (billing / payroll-error / integration / how-to), draft a reply for the two easy categories, and route the rest to the right human queue with a summary. Hard constraints from finance and legal: cost must stay under $0.04 per ticket on average, payroll-error tickets must NEVER get an automated reply (compliance — a human must answer those), and we can't add a vector database this quarter; we only have our existing Postgres and a REST helpdesk API (read ticket, post internal note, post public reply, set queue/tag). Propose the agent architecture: how many agents or LLM calls per ticket, which model tier for each step, what tools each one gets, how the compliance rule is enforced so a model mistake can't violate it, and what happens when classification confidence is low. We're a two-engineer team, so keep operability in mind.
expected_behavior: A restrained design: one or two LLM calls per ticket (cheap model for classification, optionally a second call for drafting), with the payroll-error prohibition enforced structurally — the reply-posting tool is simply not available on that path (routing logic in code, not in the prompt) — plus a low-confidence fallback to the human queue and a brief cost estimate showing the $0.04 budget holds.
failure_modes: Proposes a 5+ agent hierarchy (planner, critic, router, drafter, reviewer) that a two-engineer team can't operate and that blows the per-ticket budget
Enforces the payroll-error no-auto-reply rule only via prompt instructions instead of withholding the reply tool / gating in deterministic code
Sneaks in a vector DB, embeddings store, or RAG layer despite the explicit prohibition
Ignores the cost constraint entirely or picks the largest model for a 4-way classification step
No plan for low-confidence or ambiguous tickets — everything is assumed to classify cleanly
automatic_checks: The proposed happy-path design makes at most 3 LLM calls per ticket
Payroll-error path is enforced in deterministic code or by withholding the public-reply tool from that path, not only by prompt text
No vector database, embedding store, or RAG component is introduced
Includes an explicit low-confidence / ambiguous-classification route that sends the ticket to a human queue
States a per-ticket cost estimate, or explicitly assigns a cheap/small model tier to the classification step, referencing the $0.04/ticket budget
Only uses the four given helpdesk API capabilities (read ticket, internal note, public reply, set queue/tag) plus Postgres — no new external services
human_review_notes: Check hardest whether the compliance rule is enforced structurally (tool access / code gate) rather than by asking the model nicely.

expected_behavior: Identifies all the real defects — the assistant's own response is never appended to messages, tool results for multiple tool_use blocks must land in one user message paired by tool_use_id, swallowed exceptions leave a tool_use with no tool_result (the API rejection) and, when every tool fails, an unchanged messages list that re-sends the same request forever (the hang), plus no iteration cap and unhandled non-end_turn stop reasons like max_tokens — then gives a corrected loop that returns an error-flagged tool_result on failure instead of skipping it.
failure_modes: Rewrites the loop on top of LangChain/LangGraph or another framework despite the explicit framework-free requirement
Misses that the assistant response is never appended to the message history — the most fundamental bug
Fixes the exception swallowing by retrying or logging but still fails to emit a tool_result for the failed tool_use_id
Adds a max-iteration cap but forgets multiple tool_use blocks must be answered in a single following user message

prompt: Our nightly ETL (Airflow 2.7, Python) writes Parquet to S3 partitioned by event_date, then downstream dbt models read those partitions. Wednesday's run failed badly: the task updated the `etl_watermark` table to 2026-07-01 BEFORE writing files, then died on S3 throttling after writing only 3 of 11 partitions for that date. Thursday's run saw the watermark, skipped July 1 entirely, and processed July 2 normally. Current damage: July 1 has 3 partial partitions in S3, dbt has already built marts that include that partial day, and finance flagged July 1 revenue as ~70% low. Important detail: our Parquet filenames include a run UUID, so re-running a date ADDS files alongside old ones rather than replacing them. Design the full recovery — get July 1 correct end-to-end including downstream — decide what to do with the partial partitions already in S3, and then fix the task's ordering/write pattern so a mid-write crash can never cause a silently skipped day again. Stay within Airflow + S3 + dbt; no new orchestration or lakehouse tools.
expected_behavior: Recovery: delete/clear the 3 partial July 1 partitions first (because run-UUID filenames mean a re-run would double-count), re-run July 1 as a targeted backfill (reset watermark or explicit dated run), then rebuild the affected dbt models for that date and verify revenue volume against expectation. Prevention: invert the ordering so the watermark commits only after a successful, complete write — ideally write to a staging prefix or with a manifest/success marker and promote atomically.
failure_modes: Re-runs July 1 without removing the partial UUID-named files, silently double-counting 3 partitions
Fixes the raw S3 layer but forgets dbt already materialized marts from the partial day, leaving finance numbers wrong
Prevention keeps write-after-watermark or hand-waves 'add retries' without fixing the commit ordering
Reaches for new tooling (Iceberg/Delta, a new orchestrator) despite the explicit stack constraint
No end verification — never compares recovered July 1 volume/revenue against expected magnitude
automatic_checks: Explicitly deletes or quarantines the partial July 1 partitions BEFORE re-running, citing the run-UUID additive-write behavior as the reason
Includes a targeted re-run/backfill of July 1 only (watermark reset or explicit dated run), not a full-history reprocess
Includes rebuilding the downstream dbt models for the affected date after the raw data is fixed
Prevention changes the ordering so the watermark is updated only after all partitions are fully written (write-then-commit), e.g., staging prefix, _SUCCESS marker, or atomic promote
Stays within Airflow + S3 + dbt (no Iceberg/Delta/new orchestration tools) and includes a final verification step against expected July 1 volume
human_review_notes: Look hardest at whether the answer catches BOTH silent-failure traps: the additive UUID filenames (double-counting on re-run) and the already-built dbt marts needing rebuild.
